t: How To Deal With A Principal Who Doesn't Say Hello
q: Now, before we go any further, I want to say that such behavior is beyond the pale. It’s rude and unprofessional and there’s no excuse for it. But here’s the thing: It’s not about you.
They’re just overwhelmed. They’re so far underwater and lost in thought that you don’t even register.
But the biggest red flag is that they don’t see the value in greeting staff members, however brief—which is a clear sign of poor leadership.

Namely, interact with them only out of necessity, which if you do your job should be a rare occurrence. Be kind. Be accommodating. But keep the relationship utmost professional, need to know basis only.
When you’re confident in your own skin, when you know you’re doing right by your students and don’t need anyone’s approval, people tend to bend over backwards to give it to you anyway.
x: While he calls such behavior rude and unprofessional, he reassures readers that it is almost never personal—principals who behave this way are usually overwhelmed and avoiding interactions that might create more work…
Linsin addresses the unsettling experience of a principal who walks past staff without any acknowledgment, which can leave teachers questioning their standing or reputation.
He warns, however, that the behavior is a legitimate red flag about a principal's leadership and interpersonal skills, since staff morale depends on basic courtesies like greetings.
The recommended response is to keep the relationship strictly professional and need-to-know only.
Confidence in one's own work, detached from the need for administrative approval, tends to earn respect over time.

t: Why Focusing On Details Is Effective Teaching
q: The mistake is this: Failing to teach lessons, routines, rules, and expectations—or anything else for that matter—with enough detail.
Most teachers I observe tend to focus on the big picture. They linger on broad conceptual whats and whys because they assume that smaller, fact-heavy details are boring. But the opposite is true.
Details best prepare students to perform independently because they remove all fears, concerns, and questions over what, specifically, they need to do to succeed.
Highly detailed teaching develops strong intrinsic motivation.
So shine a light into every crook and cranny. Bridge every gap with incremental stepping stones.
x: Most teachers under-teach details; going deeper into the granular "how" is what actually helps students meet high expectations.
Contrary to common assumption, details generate more student interest and fascination than broad conceptual overviews.
Detailed instruction provides a clear roadmap, eliminating student confusion about what success requires.
Most teachers under-teach details; going deeper into the granular "how" is what actually helps students meet high expectations.
Asked what single piece of advice he would give teachers, Linsin identifies one common mistake: failing to teach lessons, routines, and expectations with enough detail.

t: A Sneaky, Hidden Reason Why You're Inconsistent https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/06/02/a-sneaky-hidden-reason-why-youre-inconsistent/
q: They were unsure what did and didn’t constitute breaking their own rules.
It didn’t feel right in the moment to enforce a consequence, but technically it was against the rules.

Not knowing where the line was caused these teachers to freeze, question themselves, and then, more often than not, do nothing at all—which inevitably would lead to other, more serious and disruptive behaviors.
The solution is to decide ahead of time exactly what is and isn’t okay, and then teach and model what that looks like to students.
You must be clear in your own mind where the boundary lines are before you can ever effectively teach them to your students or enforce them consistently.
Once your boundaries are clearly established, and non-negotiably set in stone, all awkwardness and indecision will disappear.
